fields.description: Master switch for log ingestion. Leave OFF until you have confirmed this server actually writes sshd records where the app can read them — run the facility check in CLAUDE.md first. When off, the scheduled ingest job exits immediately and writes nothing.
fields.label: Enable SSH Monitoring

fields.description: Where auth events are read from. Auto probes journald first (structured, gives a resumable cursor and the kernel audit-session id) and falls back to the auth.log text file. Pin this to a specific source only when diagnosing — a wrong pin silently stops ingestion.
fields.label: Log Source

fields.description: Read-only. What Auto actually chose on the last run, so you are never guessing which source is live. 'none' means neither journald nor auth.log was readable by the bench user.
fields.label: Detected Log Source

fields.description: Only used when the source is Auth Log. Debian/Ubuntu write /var/log/auth.log; RHEL-family systems use /var/log/secure. The bench user must be able to read it — on Ubuntu that means membership of the 'adm' group, which needs no sudo.
fields.label: Auth Log Path

fields.description: Back-pressure. A large backlog is drained across several runs rather than in one, so a brute-force burst can never make a single job exhaust memory. The checkpoint advances only as far as the records actually consumed, so nothing is skipped.
fields.label: Max Records Per Run

fields.description: How far back to read on the very first run, and after a journal cursor is lost (which happens when the journal rotates past the position we stored). Re-reading is safe: every record carries a unique dedup hash, so an overlapping window inserts nothing new.
fields.label: Bootstrap Hours

fields.description: One syslog program name per line, dropped before parsing. This is not cosmetic: on a typical box CRON's PAM session pairs are roughly three quarters of all auth-facility volume, and none of it is a login. Do NOT add 'sshd' or 'sudo' here.
fields.label: Ignore Programs

fields.description: Resolve each source IP to a country so the dashboard can show where logins come from. Turn off if this server must make no outbound requests at all; events are still recorded, they simply have no country.
fields.label: Enable Geolocation

fields.description: ip-api.com is free and needs no key. Lookups are batched 100 IPs per request and each IP is resolved once and cached forever, so the free 45-requests-per-minute limit is never approached. Private and loopback addresses are never sent anywhere.
fields.label: Resolver

fields.description: IPs per lookup request. 100 is ip-api.com's documented maximum for a single batch call; raising it will cause the provider to reject the request.
fields.label: Batch Size

fields.description: 0 means never re-resolve an IP once it has a country. Set a value only if you care about addresses being reassigned between networks, which for auditing an intrusion is rarely worth the extra requests.
fields.label: Re-resolve After (Days)

fields.description: Not needed for the free ip-api.com tier — leave blank. It exists so a paid endpoint or a MaxMind licence key can be added later without a schema change.
fields.label: Resolver API Key

fields.description: Raise a desk notification when an ingest run sees something worth a human look. Alerts are de-duplicated per rule per day, so a brute-force run of thousands of attempts produces one notification, not thousands.
fields.label: Enable Alerts

fields.description: One email address per line. Leave blank to notify every enabled System Manager, which is the safer default — an empty list here never means 'nobody gets told'.
fields.label: Alert Recipients

fields.description: Failed attempts from one IP within a single ingest window before an alert is raised. With fail2ban active most attackers are banned before reaching this, so a trigger means either fail2ban is not working or the source is distributed.
fields.label: Failed Login Threshold

fields.description: Alert the first time a SUCCESSFUL login arrives from a country never seen before. This is the highest-signal rule available: an attacker with valid credentials looks exactly like you, except for where they are.
fields.label: Alert On New Country

fields.description: Alert on any successful login as root. On a correctly hardened server (PermitRootLogin no) this is impossible, which is precisely why it is worth alerting on — it means the SSH configuration changed.
fields.label: Alert On Root Login

fields.description: One two-letter ISO country code per line (e.g. GH, DE). Logins from these never raise the new-country alert. Keep it short — every code added here is a place an attacker can log in from without you being told.
fields.label: Trusted Countries

fields.description: Safety interlock. While OFF, no App Install Request can run and nothing in this app will execute a bench command. Turn it on deliberately, and consider turning it back off once the apps you needed are installed.
fields.label: Allow App Installs

fields.description: Directory scanned for benches. Leave EMPTY to use the directory this bench sits in, which is right on almost every machine — a fixed default here would be one developer's home directory shipped to every server. A folder counts as a bench only if it contains all of apps/, sites/, config/, logs/ and config/pids.
fields.label: Bench Root

fields.description: Absolute path to the bench CLI. Must be absolute: background workers do not inherit your login shell's PATH, so a bare 'bench' will not be found.
fields.label: Bench Executable

fields.description: How long a single bench command may run before the app kills its whole process group. Raised from 30 to 60 minutes on evidence: a git pull of erpnext into a bench that had been cloned shallow (bench uses --depth 1) was still fetching at the 30-minute mark and was terminated. Large repositories with little local history are genuinely slow. Existing installs keep whatever is already saved here — change it on this form if a real operation needs longer.
fields.label: Install Timeout (Seconds)

fields.description: Exported as GIT_SSH_COMMAND for every git operation. BatchMode=yes is the load-bearing part: it turns a missing key or a passphrase prompt into an immediate error instead of a background job that hangs forever waiting for input nobody can type.
fields.label: Git SSH Command
Run Security Scans
fields.description: The persistence, account and network detectors. Off means they are not collecting — which looks exactly like a quiet server, so leaving it off is a decision worth making deliberately.

fields.label: Log Only, Do Not Alert
fields.description: Collect and record findings without raising alerts. Run a new detector this way for a week and read what it produces: an alerting system that cries wolf on day three teaches the one person who reads it to stop.

fields.label: Expect Outbound Filtering
fields.description: Tick this once a default-deny OUTPUT policy is in place. The app will then tell you if it disappears — the egress lock is the control that makes 'this cannot happen again' true for the provider, and its silent removal must not be possible.

fields.label: Forward Events To
fields.description: An HTTPS endpoint on ANOTHER machine that receives every security finding as JSON when it is raised. This is the part that makes the rest dependable: an agent on a compromised host cannot be trusted to report that host's compromise, and an attacker with root can stop the scheduler or edit the local records. The local database is a convenience; the off-box copy is the evidence.

fields.label: Forwarding Token
fields.description: Sent as a Bearer token so the collector can tell this host's events from anyone else's.

fields.label: Watchdog Token
fields.description: Lets an outside machine poll /api/method/server.api.security_heartbeat without a session, to check this host is still reporting. A watcher that runs HERE cannot notice that it has been stopped, which is the whole point of putting it elsewhere.
